text: EMR populations have been negatively affected by a number of factors, including vegetative succession (e.g. encroachment of woody-plant vegetation), habitat fragmentation, and water fluctuation (Shoemaker and Gibbs 2010; Szymanski 1998). These habitat modifications have resulted in shifts in habitat utilization of these snakes. For example, vegetative succession can cause a decrease in the prey population, which limits the size of the EMR populations that can be sustained by the habitat (Szymanski et al. 1998). Building of roads creates significant habitat fragmentation and can be directly linked to the species higher mortality rates (Szymanski et al. 2015). Additionally, these mortality rates are affected by changes in water levels. EMR live in open wetland habitats and depend on high water levels to survive during winter hibernation (Harvey and Weatherhead 2006). These fragile habitats are vulnerable to changes in water levels and successional change (Gibbs et al. 1997; Moore and Gillingham 2006). While its historical range has been slightly reduced over the last decades, the number of individuals and populations has declined significantly, with only half of the known historical populations remaining (Gibbs et al. 1997; Most of the remaining populations found in Michigan and Ontario, Canada are small and isolated (Bailey et al. 2012; Miller 2006) making them vulnerable to the impact of genetic drift (Sovic et al. 2019). Due to this decline in population numbers, the EMR was listed as 1 Department of Biology, Andrews University, Berrien Springs, MI, United States 2 Center for Craniofacial Molecular Biology, Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, United States Abstract Eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus; hereafter EMR) populations have been severely affected by factors such as vegetative succession, habitat fragmentation, and water fluctuation. This has led to a great reduction in the number of populations and population sizes, with only half of the known historical populations remaining and many projected to be decimated in the next couple of decades. Current management efforts rely primarily on visual surveys to determine population status. However, EMR are very cryptic and the current resources to manage and survey populations are insufficient for proper species assessment. Here, we propose a non-invasive method to assess presence and absence of the EMR through the genetic analysis of shed skin. Using mitochondrial DNA amplification, EMR were conclusively identified and distinguished from other allopatric snake species. The viability of this method for species identification was supported by analysis of DNA from shed skins following one month of exposure at two EMR habitats. This methodology can be paired with citizen science projects to improve the current management of EMR populations throughout their range.

Identification of the Eastern Massasauga Rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus) through genetic analysis of shed skin raised additional concern over the current management of the species (Bailey et al. 2012).

EMR, like many other reptiles and amphibians, have cryptic natural histories and are very difficult to detect in the wild (Steen 2010). Even under ideal survey conditions, detection rates can vary considerably from site to site. The standard technique currently used to survey EMR are visual surveys (Casper et al. 2001). Visual surveys for this cryptic species are challenging, mainly due to the large amount of field hours required (Moore and Gillingham 2006; Shoemaker and Gibbs 2010), and thus make the large sampling efforts needed for management and assessment very difficult. Alternative ways to assess EMR populations are needed that do not require visual identification.

Genetic analysis of shed skins can serve as a practical alternative to augment visual surveys of EMR (Rajpoot et al. 2021). Because of their sedentary nature, EMR do not move across large areas of territory and their ranges are localized to their preferred habitat types (e.g. grasslands, wet prairies, swamps, etc.) Although EMR habitats vary seasonally, there are two main factors that characterize them: open areas with light and shade and accessibility to a water table close to the surface (Szymanski 1998). While these components will largely determine the decay of shed skins, other factors such as presence of insects, precipitation, and amount of sunlight can also affect the decay level. Knowledge of the decay rates of DNA in EMR sheds exposed to natural habitats can help to determine the usefulness of sheds as indicators of EMR presence.

Here, we propose a non-invasive method to assess presence and absence of EMR through the genetic analysis of shed skin. Using mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) amplification, we show that EMR can be conclusively identified and distinguished from other allopatric snake species. We also investigate the decay rates of DNA in EMR sheds at two of their preferred habitats, with results suggesting that while EMR skins decay over time, they continued to yield mtDNA sufficient to identify EMR even after several weeks. As anecdotal reports of EMR sightings from citizen scientists can be very unreliable, this proposed methodology could support visual surveys to provide hard evidence on continued presence.

All sheds were collected in natural habitats in southwest Michigan from areas of known or suspected EMR presence (Table 1). Shed skins were visually inspected and rated based on condition (Undegraded- no visible decay;

Slightly degraded- some level of decay, but still retaining structure; Highly degraded – heavy decay). Sheds were then identified as either confirmed EMR (single subcaudal ventral scales or evidence of rattle), non-EMR (split subcaudal ventral scales, length or girth outside of the known range for EMR or the terminal end showed no evidence of a rattle), or Unknown and stored at -80 °C. Six skins were confirmed EMR, while the rest included other species found in the area or were unknown (Table 1). In addition, blood samples were extracted from the caudal vein of two wild EMR using standard methods (see Hall 2019). Collection and handling of EMR sheds and blood were conducted under State (Michigan DNR Permit) and federal (USFWS Permit #TE29691C-0 to DGS) permits.

DNA extraction was performed as described previously (Eguchi and Eguchi 2000). Briefly, a portion of each shed skin (50 mg) was cut into small pieces with scissors. To prevent cross-contamination, scissors and gloves were wiped down with 70% ethanol after handling each skin and gloves were changed frequently. Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was added to cover skin and samples were briefly washed by shaking vigorously. PBS was discarded and 1.5 ml of cell dispersion solution (200 mM Tris/HCl, pH 8.0, 1.5 mg/ ml collagenase from Clostridium histolyticum (Sigma)) was added. The samples were shaken at 300 rpm and 37 °C for 24 h. After carefully discarding the supernatant, 1.5 ml of TE buffer (10 mM Tris/HCl, pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA) containing 0.1% SDS and 0.6 mg/ml Proteinase K from Tritirachium album (Sigma) was added. The samples were again shaken at 300 rpm and 37 °C for 24 h. The supernatants were transferred to new tubes and DNA isolated using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen). The same kit was used to purify DNA from blood samples. PCR reactions to amplify nuclear or mitochondrial DNA extracted from both shed skins and EMR blood samples (positive controls) were performed in 50 μl reaction volumes. Each PCR reaction contained 0.25 μl DreamTaq DNA Polymerase (Thermofisher), 2mM dNTP mix, 1 μl template DNA and 0.15 μM of each primer. A pit viper-specific primer pair was used to amplify intronic DNA within the TATA box-binding protein (TBP) locus (Table 2; Creer et al. 2005) and EMR-specific primers were used for amplification of regions within the mitochondrial cytochrome b (Cytb) and control region 1 (Cr1) loci (Table 2; Pearce 2001). The PCR cycle was performed on a BioRad T100 thermocycler, and included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 50–54 °C (see Table 2) for 30 s, and 72 °C for 60 s, and a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min.

Following PCR, products were visualized on 2% agarose gels along with 100-bp DNA Ladder (ThermoFisher). Sanger dideoxy sequencing of PCR products was performed by Genscript (Piscataway, NJ). Forward PCR primers were used for sequencing. This sequencing of PCR products confirmed the EMR identity of successful PCR reactions.

Three undegraded confirmed EMR sheds were used for the skin decay analysis. Two fragments of each shed weighing 0.3 g each were placed into a sealed plastic bag. Scissors and tweezers were sprayed with 70% EtOH to avoid crosscontamination. The specimens were kept at room temperature during transportation to the field site. The field site was located in a farming area in southwest Michigan with restricted access. Presence of EMR at this site was confirmed previously (Hall 2019). The field site was surveyed prior to experimental set up and two locations representative of EMR habitat were selected. The first location exhibited characteristics of open prairie fen, including tall grasses and direct exposure to sunlight (Fig. 1 A). The second location was located nearby in an upland woodland habitat, presenting semi-moist ground covered in leaves (Fig. 1 C).

Upon arrival at the designated locations, each skin shed sample was removed from the sealed plastic bag with tweezers and placed within its separate compartment in the wire cage, which was in direct contact with the ground (See Fig. 1B and D). The tweezers were sprayed with 70% ethanol after handling each skin. At 5, 10, 20, and 30 days a small fragment of each skin shed (approximately 2 × 2 cm) was collected and transported back to the lab, where it was stored at -80 °C. Upon thawing, the skin specimens were weighed and subsequently trimmed so that their weights would be 0.05 g ± 0.003 g. DNA was extracted and isolated using the method described above (see “DNA extraction and isolation” section).

Amplifications of the Cytb mtDNA locus were obtained through SYBR green chemistry using a BioRad CFX96 thermocycler. Each 20 μL qPCR reaction contained 10 μl SsoAdvanced Universal SYBR Green Supermix (BioRad), 2 μl template DNA, and 0.5 μM of each primer (Cytb15810L and CytbH). The reactions were run in duplicate, with the addition of a positive control (S007, an EMR-positive skin) and a negative control (water).

After isolation of DNA from shed skins, the DNA was resolved on a 1% agarose gel (Fig. 2 A). The DNA typically presented as a smear mostly 10,000 bp or smaller. Some of the samples exhibited a distinct band approximately 20,000 bp in size. In order to determine if DNA size and quantity corresponded to the quality or identity of the collected skin, we performed DNA quantification and analysis with ImageJ. No difference was observed in the size distribution of DNA isolated from EMR and non-EMR shed skin as expected. Therefore, the mitochondrial Cytb and control region 1 loci were targeted in PCR, and products resolved on a 2% agarose gel (Fig. Amplification of both loci produced bands of the expected sizes for all known EMR specimens (S006-S008; S010-S012), confirming the species-specific nature of these primers. No amplification of Cytb was observed using DNA from non-EMR or unknown shed skins. All non-EMR and unknown samples, except S003, presented a band smaller than the expected size using Cr1 primers; this is likely a primer dimer occurring in the absence of specific template binding. Bands of similar sizes were seen when template DNA from EMR blood was used as a positive control (not shown). The sequences of Cr1 and Cytb products were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, further indicating their EMR origin. Because no specific bands were obtained for any of our unknown samples, these results suggest that our unknown samples were not EMR.

The age of a shed skin is a relevant piece of information, indicating how long it has been since the EMR was present. Our visual analysis of shed skin quality did not correspond to the quality or quantity of DNA that could be extracted from the skin (compare Table 1; Fig. 2). To determine the ng/μl, while that isolated from non-EMR shed skins had a concentration that was not significantly different (2.83 ng/ μl, independent sample t-test p = 0.62). Likewise, the mean concentration of DNA less than 10,000 bp in size was also not significantly different between EMRs and non-EMRs (145.5 ng/μl and 130.3 ng/μl respectively, independent sample t-test p = 0.55). No relationship was observed between DNA quality as determined by agarose gel electrophoresis (Fig. 2 A) and skin condition (Table 2). This suggests that the physical appearance of skins might not directly indicate the actual time since shedding, but rather reflect other habitat dependent factors like moisture, pH, or temperature.

Amplification of intronic and mitochondrial DNA for species identification Previous studies have used the nucleotide diversity found within introns to identify snake species by PCR. In these cases, the high conservation of exons was used for primer attachment (Creer et al. 2005). In order to test this approach, we attempted amplification of a portion of the TBP gene. This amplification presented a faint band at the expected size of 796 bp for a few samples, while most amplifications resulted in bands of variable size including 150 and 200 bp (not shown). This approach was not further pursued due to inconsistency in the results.

The improper management of remnant EMR populations has called into question the reliability of traditional survey methods, particularly regarding their contribution to the conservation of this elusive species. Interestingly, a substantial portion of the historical EMR populations continue to have an unknown status because of the difficulty in detecting the viability of a molecular identification of EMR using shed skin of varying ages and exposures, we performed a controlled field study of skin decay. We also used this opportunity to assess any potential differences in the decay of skins between grassland and woodland habitats.

Many hours of field survey could potentially be eliminated. Other studies have used similar techniques using bird feathers (Eguchi and Eguchi 2000) and mammals hairs (Onorato et al. 2010). This application should be further investigated as it would aid in the mapping of active EMR populations.

The present study also uses PCR technology to quantify the decay of skin DNA and suggests a means of determining time since shedding. Preliminary findings of this study suggest that the decay of skin DNA may vary considerably depending on the environmental characteristics of the shedding location, and that this variation is notable within the first days post-shedding. We hypothesize that the greater decay observed at the grassland site may be attributed to various factors such as warmer temperature, sunlight, and rainfall; nonetheless, we acknowledge that the factors responsible for the differential degradation of skin DNA in grassland and woodland sites are outside the scope of this study. What is clear is that shed skins confirm presence of EMR on the order of days or weeks.

Overall, we conclude that genetic analysis of EMR skin sheds can be a useful method to survey this elusive species, especially over a large area. This method could be especially effective if combined with citizen science projects in areas of suspected or known EMR presence. Land managers could provide instructions to visitors on how to carefully collect any shed skins that they may find and submit them for genetic analysis.

Current protocols in EMR population management require there be no detection of EMR over 15 years in order to be classified as extirpated from a location. This also requires a minimum of 40 survey hours per year due to the low detectability rate of EMR (Casper et al. 2001). This low detectability rate poses a challenge to manage and monitor continued presence at a site.

One way to improve the detection probability of rare and cryptic species is to pair visual surveys with auxiliary data (Durso and Seigel 2015; Kucherenko et al. 2018). Auxiliary data can include capture and telemetry data (Moore and Gillingham 2006), passive detection through PIT (passive integrated transmission) tags (Jemison et al. 1995), molecular detection from the environment (Ratsch et al. 2020), and the compilation of visual sightings by citizen scientists (Bertram et al. 2001). Currently, most of these methods have complications for EMR studies. Telemetry and the use of PIT tags require capture and release, which is not feasible for large scale (statewide) presence/absence monitoring. Environmental DNA (eDNA) has been shown to be an effective tool for detection of other terrestrial snakes (Kucherenko et al. 2018); however, this technology has not yet been demonstrated to be logistically or financially viable for EMR (Baker et al. 2020). Although the use of sightings from citizen scientists has great potential, it has major limitations for EMR due to the confusion with similar looking snakes within their habitats.

To contribute to current conservation efforts of EMR, we propose the use of an identification method based on the genetic analysis of shed skins. We show that an EMRspecific primer pair can be used to identify and distinguish EMRs from other allopatric species in southwest Michigan.
